sourceDocuments.name: WHATWG HTML Living Standard: disabled controls and constraint validation
sourceDocuments.text:
Source: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html (accessed 2026-09-06). Paraphrased guidance:

An input's disabled attribute disables it whenever present, regardless of its string value. An input is also disabled by a fieldset ancestor with that attribute, except when inside that fieldset's first legend element child. Evaluate this exception separately for each fieldset ancestor: exemption from one does not remove another qualifying ancestor or the input's own attribute. Removing the input's attribute therefore need not enable it. Disabled controls are barred from constraint validation. A datalist ancestor is another barring condition; these examples are not an exhaustive list. willValidate is true exactly when the element is a candidate for constraint validation. checkValidity() returns false when a candidate fails its constraints and fires invalid; otherwise it returns true. Consequently, true does not prove that a barred control's value satisfies its constraints. Disabling does not prevent every modification: JavaScript can still change value or checkedness. These rules apply to the current DOM state; changes to attributes or ancestry can change the result.

prompt:
An input element #x exists in the following markup:

<fieldset disabled id="fs">
  <legend>Title</legend>
  <input id="x" type="text" disabled required value="">
</fieldset>

A script then runs:
  document.getElementById('x').removeAttribute('disabled');

After the script executes, what is the effective state of #x?
choices: Still disabled, because the disabled fieldset ancestor still applies
Enabled, because its own disabled attribute was removed
Enabled, because removeAttribute always overrides inherited disabling
Still disabled, but only until the browser recalculates layout

prompt: A disabled outer fieldset's first legend contains a disabled inner fieldset that has no legend child. Inside the inner fieldset is <input id='x'> with no own disabled attribute. Which statement correctly describes #x's disabled status and why?
choices: Disabled — exempt from the outer fieldset, but the inner fieldset still disables it
Not disabled — the outer's first-legend exception covers everything inside that legend
Disabled — both fieldsets disable it because nested legends never stack exceptions
Not disabled — the inner fieldset inherits the exemption granted by the outer's first legend

sourceDocuments.text:

prompt:
Consider this HTML structure:

<fieldset disabled>
  <legend>
    <fieldset disabled>
      <legend><input id="A"></legend>
      <input id="B">
    </fieldset>
  </legend>
  <input id="C">
</fieldset>

None of the inputs have their own disabled attribute. Which correctly describes the effective disabled state of A, B, and C?
choices: A is enabled; B is disabled; C is disabled
A is enabled; B is enabled; C is disabled
A is disabled; B is disabled; C is disabled
A is enabled; B is disabled; C is enabled
